changed-modified-data

changed-modified-data.Rmd

Motivation

When we receive an updated version of a dataset, dfdiffs helps us answer three questions:

  1. What rows are here now that weren’t here before?
  2. What rows were here before that aren’t here now?
  3. What values have been changed?

This vignette covers the two functions that answer the third question: create_changed_data() and create_modified_data(). Both are built on the same base R engine (diff_values_by_key() and compare_values()), and they differ only in the shape of their output:

  • create_changed_data() returns $num_diffs and $var_diffs, which are used by compare_data().
  • create_modified_data() returns $diffs_byvar and $diffs, which are used by mod_compare and create_comparison_report().

Packages 

library(dfdiffs)
library(arsenal) # comparedf, for comparison

Example data

We’ll use two datasets from the package to test what’s been modified.

Initial Data

InitialData is the base (original) dataset:

InitialData <- dfdiffs::InitialData
InitialData
subject_id record text_value_a text_value_b created_date updated_date entered_date
A 1 Issue unresolved Fatigue 2021-07-29 2021-09-29 2021-09-29
A 2 Issue unresolved Fatigue 2021-07-29 2021-10-03 2021-10-29
B 3 Issue resolved Fever 2021-07-16 2021-09-02 2021-08-18
C 4 Issue resolved Joint pain 2021-08-24 2021-10-03 2021-10-03
C 5 Issue resolved Joint pain 2021-08-24 2021-09-20 2021-10-20

Changed Data

ChangedData is the dataset we’ll compare against InitialData:

ChangedData <- dfdiffs::ChangedData
ChangedData
subject_id record text_value_a text_value_b created_date updated_date entered_date
A 1 Issue resolved Fatigue 2021-07-29 2021-10-03 2021-11-30
A 2 Issue resolved Fatigue 2021-07-29 2021-11-27 2021-11-30
B 3 Issue resolved Fever 2021-07-16 2021-10-20 2021-11-21
C 4 Issue resolved Joint pain, stiffness and swelling 2021-08-24 2021-10-13 2021-11-11
C 5 Issue resolved Joint pain 2021-08-24 2021-10-14 2021-11-16

Creating join columns

We’ll use create_new_column() to build a join_var column from subject_id and record in both datasets:

ChangedDataJoin <- create_new_column(
  data = ChangedData,
  cols = c("subject_id", "record"),
  new_name = "join_var")
InitialDataJoin <- create_new_column(
  data = InitialData,
  cols = c("subject_id", "record"),
  new_name = "join_var")

ChangedDataJoin now starts with the new join_var column:

ChangedDataJoin
join_var subject_id record text_value_a text_value_b created_date updated_date entered_date

A-2 A 2 Issue resolved Fatigue 2021-07-29 2021-11-27 2021-11-30
B-3 B 3 Issue resolved Fever 2021-07-16 2021-10-20 2021-11-21
C-4 C 4 Issue resolved Joint pain, stiffness and swelling 2021-08-24 2021-10-13 2021-11-11
C-5 C 5 Issue resolved Joint pain 2021-08-24 2021-10-14 2021-11-16

create_changed_data()

Arguments

create_changed_data() takes the same compare, base, by, by_col, and cols arguments as create_new_data(). The reference table in that vignette lists every combination.

The difference is what the function does with matched rows. create_new_data() and create_deleted_data() find rows with no match, but create_changed_data() compares the values within matched rows, column by column.

Call structure

create_changed_data() is built on diff_values_by_key(), a base R engine that uses compare_values() to compare matched rows column by column. It also uses the same rename_join_col() and create_new_column() helpers as the other comparison functions. The call tree below was generated from the package source with stackcallr (pak::pak("mjfrigaard/stackcallr")). Only functions defined in dfdiffs are shown.

stackcallr::call_tree_dir("R", root = "create_changed_data")
█─create_changed_data
├─select_cols
├─█─diff_values_by_key
│ ├─compare_values
│ └─class_diffs
├─rename_join_col
├─create_new_column
└─class_diffs

Worked examples

No by column: row-by-row comparison

When we supply only the two datasets, create_changed_data() compares them row by row. The $num_diffs and $var_diffs tables are shown side by side below:

create_changed_data(
  compare = ChangedData,
  base = InitialData)
Variable name Modified Values
subject_id 0
record 0
text_value_a 2
text_value_b 1
created_date 0
updated_date 5
entered_date 5

updated_date 2 2021-11-27 2021-10-03

entered_date 2 2021-11-30 2021-10-29

entered_date 4 2021-11-11 2021-10-03
entered_date 5 2021-11-16 2021-10-20

A single by column

Passing join_var as the by column matches rows on that key instead of on row position:

create_changed_data(
  compare = ChangedDataJoin,
  base = InitialDataJoin,
  by = "join_var")

Multiple by columns, a new by_col, and cols

This is the most complete case. The by columns are combined into a single key named with by_col, and only the columns in cols are compared:

create_changed_data(
  compare = ChangedData,
  base = InitialData,
  by = c("subject_id", "record"),
  by_col = "join",
  cols = c("text_value_a", "text_value_b"))
Variable name Modified Values
text_value_a 2
text_value_b 1
Variable name join Current Value Previous Value
text_value_a A-1 Issue resolved Issue unresolved
text_value_a A-2 Issue resolved Issue unresolved
text_value_b C-4 Joint pain, stiffness and swelling Joint pain

create_modified_data()

create_modified_data() answers the same question as create_changed_data(), but its output is shaped for the “Review Changes” report instead of compare_data().

arsenal::comparedf(), for comparison

Before version 2.1.0, create_modified_data() was built directly on arsenal::comparedf(). To see where the current output comes from, we’ll run arsenal::comparedf() on the same data:

modified_cdf <- arsenal::comparedf(
  x = ChangedDataJoin,
  y = InitialDataJoin,
  by = "join_var")
modified_cdf_sum <- summary(modified_cdf)

The summary contains several tables, but we’re only interested in diffs.byvar.table and diffs.table:

modified_cdf_sum$diffs.byvar.table
var.x var.y n NAs
subject_id subject_id 0 0
record record 0 0
text_value_a text_value_a 2 0
text_value_b text_value_b 1 0
created_date created_date 0 0
updated_date updated_date 5 0
entered_date entered_date 5 0
modified_cdf_sum$diffs.table
var.x var.y join_var values.x values.y row.x row.y
text_value_a text_value_a A-1 Issue re…. Issue un…. 1 1
text_value_a text_value_a A-2 Issue re…. Issue un…. 2 2
text_value_b text_value_b C-4 Joint pa…. Joint pain 4 4
updated_date updated_date A-1 2021-10-03 2021-09-29 1 1
updated_date updated_date A-2 2021-11-27 2021-10-03 2 2
updated_date updated_date B-3 2021-10-20 2021-09-02 3 3
updated_date updated_date C-4 2021-10-13 2021-10-03 4 4
updated_date updated_date C-5 2021-10-14 2021-09-20 5 5
entered_date entered_date A-1 2021-11-30 2021-09-29 1 1
entered_date entered_date A-2 2021-11-30 2021-10-29 2 2
entered_date entered_date B-3 2021-11-21 2021-08-18 3 3
entered_date entered_date C-4 2021-11-11 2021-10-03 4 4
entered_date entered_date C-5 2021-11-16 2021-10-20 5 5

create_modified_data() returns only a small fraction of this output, reshaped into $diffs_byvar and $diffs. The extra var.y column is dropped, var.x becomes Variable name, and values.x and values.y become Current Value and Previous Value. The row position columns (row.x and row.y) are also dropped in favor of the join key.

We can see the reshaped output by running create_modified_data() on the same joined datasets:

modified <- create_modified_data(
  compare = ChangedDataJoin,
  base = InitialDataJoin,
  by = "join_var")
modified$diffs_byvar

text_value_b 1

create_modified_data() takes the same compare, base, by, by_col, and cols arguments as create_new_data() and create_changed_data(). The reference table lists every combination.

Call structure

create_modified_data() is built on the same diff_values_by_key() engine as create_changed_data(). The call tree below was generated with stackcallr (pak::pak("mjfrigaard/stackcallr")). Only functions defined in dfdiffs are shown.
